newsitem.title: SPAIN: NATO emerges as centrepiece of new security order.
newsitem.headline: NATO emerges as centrepiece of new security order.

text.p: In the twilight of a brutal century, the Western powers are piecing together a new European security system which they hope will stop war returning to the continent's blood-drenched soil.

But as the new millenium dawns, the dream of peace faces enormous challenges from both within and without the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) -- the Cold War victor around which the new architecture is being assembled.

A NATO summit on Tuesday signalled the start of a new era, formally erasing Europe's Cold War division by inviting former communist foes Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to slip under the U.S.-led alliance's protective cloak.

On Wednesday NATO leaders signed a special charter with Ukraine to run parallel to a NATO-Russia pact, signed last May, and then inaugurated a new organisation boosting security links with 28 partnership states from Europe and Eurasia.

"Madrid 1997 will undoubtably go down in history as a city where the dividing line left by the Cold War in the centre of Europe was eliminated," Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma said as he signed the document.
The "Charter on a Distinctive Partnership between NATO and Ukraine" gives Kiev the right to call "consultations" with NATO if it faces an outside threat.

"We understand perfectly well the realities that we have on the European continent and these are the reasons for our cooperation with NATO," Kuchma said of the charter which seeks to build closer ties with the West without alarming Russia.

NATO hopes the charter, the NATO-Russia Founding Act, under which Moscow grudgingly accepted the alliance's eastwards expansion, and the partnership council -- aspiring NATO members and those with no membership ambitions -- will knit the continent in a web of overlapping alliances.

"We can transform this continent into a safer and more stable place where each country can live and work with each other in peace and prosperity," NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said at the inauguration of the new Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council.

Present in all organisations and the motor pushing the entire enterprise is the world's only superpower, the United States -- the country which ensured NATO was the most powerful military alliance ever assembled.

"NATO today is the symbol of the U.S. will to remain present in Europe as a European power," Dominique Moisi of the French Institute for International Relations told Reuters. "It is the insurance policy from all the uncertainties of life."

The bitter experience of the wars in former Yugoslavia, which Europe failed to prevent and could only stop with real U.S. engagement, convinced governments on both sides of the Atlantic that America had to continue to play the pivotal role.
"The failure of Bosnia only highlights that, the less Europe exists, the less there is an alternative to America in Europe," Moisi added.
But U.S. taxpayers, backed by rightwing populist politicians, do not currently agree.

U.S. President Bill Clinton accepted as he arrived in Madrid that he had a fight on his hands to win ratification of enlargement from a sceptical Republican-led Congress and explain why U.S. troops were being pledged to protect faraway lands.

Leading rightwingers who saw the collapse of communism as reducing the need for U.S. involvement in Europe, warn that enlargement will weaken NATO and point accusing fingers at Europeans for not taking more responsibility for their own defence.
They argue the policy is a mistake and will alienate Russia, undermine arms agreements, destabilise countries left out and ultimately have completely the opposite effect to that intended.

The European Union, which has already come under fire for its own laggardly enlargement process, will now be watched carefully to see how much of the cost of the new security order it is prepared to bear.

Independent analysts say the question of the continued neutrality of three EU states, Finland, Sweden and Ireland, will now come to the fore. But wary electorates may not allow their governments to abandon historically-popular positions.
"Failure to abandon neutrality, which is outmoded, while benefiting from U.S.-provided security could spark new transatlantic tensions," one analyst said.
"The U.S. may now be tied to Europe, but the debate on what type of security relationship should ultimately exist between the NATO and the EU has yet to start," he added.

Advocates of both expansions say the twin processes will spread stability in Europe by supporting the new democracies and extending the West's zone of stability towards turbulent areas, such as the Balkans, Central Asia and the Black Sea rim.
But they admit that success or failure could ultimately be decided by factors way beyond the control of Western capitals -- the success of the reform process in Russia.
"If Russia succeeds and becomes a real, functioning democracy it is hard to see any threat to the new order. If it fails, well...," said one senior alliance official
